evidence.claim: Water transport shaped the towns before the highway took its present course. At Lockport, a canal intended to connect Bayou Terrebonne with New Orleans opened in 1847, followed three years later by locks at Bayou Lafourche. The bayou itself changed in 1904, when a dam severed its natural connection to the Mississippi River. A pumping station began supplying water in 1950.

evidence.claim: Lockport’s name belongs to an ambitious canal connection.
evidence.quote: Eventually, the village's name would become Lockport.

evidence.claim: William Field donated land on both banks of Bayou Lafourche to the Barataria and Lafourche Canal Company, which agreed to connect Bayou Terrebonne with New Orleans.
evidence.quote: later donated 5 arpents of it on both banks of Bayou Lafourche to Barataria and Lafourche Canal Company. As part of the transaction, the company agreed to build a canal, which would link Bayou Terrebonne to New Orleans.

evidence.claim: The canal opened in 1847 and its locks followed in 1850.
evidence.quote: At first the canal, completed in 1847, brought prosperity to the area. Three years later locks were completed at the point where the canal reached Bayou Lafourche.

evidence.claim: Shipping stayed brisk until 1868; afterward, part of the waterway fell out of use.
evidence.quote: Shipping along the canal was brisk until 1868. After that time, part of the waterway was no longer in use.

evidence.claim: A crevasse partially destroyed the locks in 1876, leaving brick bulwark remnants that remain visible beneath weeds.
evidence.quote: The crevasse of 1876 partially destroyed the locks. Today remnants of the brick bulwark are still visible under a blanket of weeds.

evidence.claim: Later, Highway 1 moved off Main Street, and businesses along its new route became the town’s commercial center.
evidence.quote: Highway 1 no longer ran along Main Street. Several businesses sprang up along the new route, and that area has become the business hub of the town.

evidence.claim: Survivors of the Chenier Caminada Hurricane founded this community in November 1893.
evidence.quote: The city was founded in November, 1893 by survivors of the Chenier Caminada Hurricane.

evidence.claim: First called Orange City, it was renamed for Pierre Charles Lee and his wife, Rosalie Albarado.
evidence.quote: The city was first named Orange City but was changed to Leevile in honor of Pierre Charles Lee and his wife Rosalie Albarado.

evidence.claim: By 1938, Leeville had 297 producing oil wells.
evidence.quote: In 1938, Leeville became the oil producing capital of Lafourche Parish with 297 producing wells.

evidence.claim: Studies by the Barataria-Terrebonne National Estuary Program found that around 70 percent of the surrounding wetlands had vanished since 1932.
evidence.quote: According to studies by the Barataria-Terrebonne National Estuary Program, around 70% of the town's surrounding wetlands have vanished since 1932

evidence.claim: The highway arrives on a barrier island where hardwood trees grow on slightly elevated ridges.
evidence.quote: Chenier forests consist of hardwood trees, primarily oaks and hackberries, as well as a variety of other vegetation such as mulberry, honeylocust, water oak, green ash, and American elm, all which grow along slightly elevated ridges.

evidence.claim: These chenier forests provide resting places for birds before or after their flight across the Gulf of Mexico.
evidence.quote: The cover of a chenier forest provides for migratory birds a place to rest before or after making the flight across the Gulf of Mexico

evidence.claim: The ridges formed as sediment accumulated during shifts of the Mississippi River’s delta.
evidence.quote: These ridges are the result of the build-up of sediment from periodic shifts of the Mississippi River's delta

evidence.claim: That small difference in elevation also helps the forests act as a barrier to saltwater intrusion into marshes during storm surges.
evidence.quote: chenier forests not only allow for the growth of hardwood trees that support the variety of migratory birds that pass through Grand Isle, but also act as a barrier for salt water intrusion into a marsh during storm surges.

evidence.claim: Grand Isle State Park occupies the island’s eastern tip.
evidence.quote: Grand Isle State Park, lies at the eastern tip of Grand Isle

evidence.claim: Oaks and hackberries are the principal trees in these forests, which occupy higher ground within a landscape of marsh and beach.
